questions.subject: ACCOUNTING
questions.stem: Case 8201: For Hawthorne Company, beginning retained earnings were $3,700, net income was $7,600, and dividends declared were $150. What are ending retained earnings?

options.misconception: reverses the effect of both income and dividends
subtracts net income from retained earnings
adds dividends instead of subtracting them

questions.explanation: Ending retained earnings begins with the opening balance, adds net income because it increases accumulated earnings, and subtracts dividends because they distribute earnings to owners, giving $11,150. Adding dividends would treat a distribution as a source of earnings.
questions.hint: Income adds to retained earnings; dividends reduce it.

questions.subject: ACCOUNTING
questions.stem: Case 8202: On its balance sheet, Hawthorne Works lists accounts payable of $3,350, accrued liabilities of $14,100, and unearned revenue of $250. What are total current liabilities?

options.misconception: reports only the smallest liability balance
subtracts one liability from another
omits unearned revenue from the current liability total

questions.explanation: Every obligation due within a year belongs in current liabilities, so $3,350 plus $14,100 plus $250 totals $17,700. Omitting unearned revenue would understate obligations because that balance represents a duty to deliver goods or services.
questions.hint: Add every obligation that must be settled within one year.

questions.subject: ACCOUNTING
questions.stem: Case 8203: Kestrel Supply issues a $3,000 bond paying 6 percent annual interest. What is the annual cash interest payment?

options.misconception: divides by the rate instead of multiplying by it

uses sixty percent instead of six percent of face value

questions.explanation: Cash interest on a bond equals face value times the stated rate, so $3,000 times six percent is $180 each year. Dividing by the rate or using the face value ignores how a coupon payment is calculated.

questions.stem: Case 8204: A $2,650 bond issued at a discount pays $13,050 of cash interest this period and has $450 of discount amortization. What is interest expense?

subtracts discount amortization from cash interest

questions.stem: Case 8280: For Larkspur Enterprises, beginning retained earnings were $4,150, net income was $1,250, and dividends declared were $400. What are ending retained earnings?

options.misconception: subtracts net income from retained earnings
adds dividends instead of subtracting them
reverses the effect of both income and dividends

questions.explanation: Ending retained earnings begins with the opening balance, adds net income because it increases accumulated earnings, and subtracts dividends because they distribute earnings to owners, giving $5,000. Adding dividends would treat a distribution as a source of earnings.
questions.hint: Income adds to retained earnings; dividends reduce it.

questions.subject: ACCOUNTING
questions.stem: Case 8281: Birchfield Company issues a $3,800 bond paying 6 percent annual interest. What is the annual cash interest payment?

options.misconception: divides by the rate instead of multiplying by it
uses sixty percent instead of six percent of face value
treats the face value itself as the interest payment

questions.explanation: Cash interest on a bond equals face value times the stated rate, so $3,800 times six percent is $228 each year. Dividing by the rate or using the face value ignores how a coupon payment is calculated.
questions.hint: Multiply face value by the stated coupon rate.

questions.stem: Case 8282: A $3,450 bond issued at a discount pays $14,250 of cash interest this period and has $600 of discount amortization. What is interest expense?

options.misconception: uses only cash interest and ignores the discount amortization

questions.explanation: When bonds are issued at a discount, interest expense exceeds the cash paid because the discount amortization is an additional financing cost, so $14,250 plus $600 gives $14,850. Subtracting the amortization would describe a premium bond instead.
questions.hint: A discount increases interest expense above the cash paid.

questions.stem: Case 8285: On May 17, 2025, the board of Harborview Partners declares a $2,400 cash dividend to be paid later. Which entry records the declaration?

options.misconception: credits the wrong account while leaving the debit unchanged
reverses the debit and credit sides of the entry

questions.explanation: Declaration creates an obligation, so Dividends is debited for $2,400 and Dividends Payable is credited. Cash is not credited at declaration because no payment has occurred yet; the cash entry is made on the payment date.

questions.stem: Case 8286: On June 12, 2026, Pinecrest Services repurchases its own shares from investors for $2,050 in cash. What entry records the treasury stock purchase?

options.text: Debit Treasury Stock $2,050; credit Dividends Payable $2,050.
options.misconception: credits the wrong account while leaving the debit unchanged
reverses the debit and credit sides of the entry
debits the wrong account while leaving the credit unchanged

questions.explanation: A repurchase of the company's own shares is recorded by debiting Treasury Stock, a contra-equity account, for $2,050 and crediting Cash. Common Stock is not reduced because the shares are not retired, and no liability arises in a repurchase.
